title: Gujarat Wins GI Tag for Unjha Cumin, Reigniting Rivalry With Rajasthan Over India's Most Prized Spice
excerpt: The Geographical Indication tag for Unjha jeera gives Gujarat exclusive branding rights over cumin, even as Rajasthan's Thar Desert produces what experts call the world's most flavorful variety.
body:
• Gujarat's Unjha cumin and fennel received Geographical Indication (GI) tags from India's GI Registry in March 2026, officially branding them as products of the Unjha region
  • Gujarat accounts for nearly 80% of India's cumin and spice seed exports, with Mehsana district alone exporting ₹3,995 crore worth of spices to 101 countries in 2024-25
  • GI-tagged products can command a 20-30% price premium, potentially disadvantaging Rajasthan's farmers whose cumin is often traded through Gujarat's Unjha market
  • India is the world's largest producer and exporter of cumin, with Rajasthan and Gujarat together dominating global supply

The Tag That Changes Everything

In the world of Indian spices, few battles run as deep — or as aromatic — as the one between Gujarat and Rajasthan over jeera. And Gujarat just scored a decisive win.

The Geographical Indications Registry granted GI tags to Unjha Cumin and Unjha Fennel in March 2026, officially certifying these spices as products originating from the Unjha region of north Gujarat's Mehsana district. The certification, announced by the Gujarat government on July 14, provides legal protection against misuse of the products' geographical identity and positions them as premium certified brands in global markets.

For Gujarat, it is a validation of Unjha's status as home to one of Asia's largest spice markets. For Rajasthan — India's second-largest cumin producer, whose farmers grow arguably the world's finest cumin in the searing Thar Desert — the tag raises an uncomfortable question: what happens when your spice gets branded as someone else's?

Gujarat's Unjha: The Trading Powerhouse

Unjha's claim to the GI tag rests on its role as a trading and processing hub. The town's Agricultural Produce Market Committee (APMC) is the principal marketplace where cumin from across Gujarat — and crucially, from neighboring Rajasthan — is channeled, graded, and exported, according to The Hindu BusinessLine.

Gujarat accounts for nearly 80% of India's cumin and spice seed exports. Mehsana district alone exported ₹3,995 crore worth of spices to 101 countries in 2024-25, according to government data. The GI tag formalizes what the trade already knows: Unjha is where the money moves.

"The GI tags mark a historic milestone for the farmers of Unjha and the region's spice trade. This will further strengthen the authenticity and market credibility of both products."

— Dinesh Patel, Chairman, Unjha Agricultural Produce Market Committee

Rajasthan's Counter: The Desert Advantage

But production quality is a different story. Rajasthan's arid western districts — Jalore, Barmer, and Jaisalmer — produce cumin that spice experts consider the world's finest. The extreme temperature swings of the Thar Desert — freezing winter nights followed by blistering spring days — force the cumin plant to concentrate its defensive compounds, particularly cuminaldehyde, the chemical responsible for that signature earthy punch.

Unjha's cumin seeds typically test at 2-3% volatile oil content. Premium harvests from Rajasthan's Jalore district in 2026 have tested as high as 4.5%, according to trade data — meaning more flavor per gram and longer shelf life for ground powders.

Rajasthan also leads in residue-free cumin production. The South Asia Biotechnology Centre in Jodhpur has been running an integrated pest management program that produces 15,000-16,000 tonnes of IPM cumin annually, procured directly from farm gates in arid villages by the world's largest spice companies at a 20-25% premium above market price.

The Diaspora Connection

For the millions of Indians abroad who stock their pantries with jeera, the GI tag debate is more than academic. GI certification allows products to command 20-30% higher prices, according to the Gujarat government. If Unjha-branded cumin captures the premium export market, Rajasthan's farmers — many of them smallholders in some of India's poorest districts — could find themselves selling the world's best cumin at commodity prices while Gujarat's traders capture the brand premium.

Rajasthan has not yet filed its own GI application for Thar Desert cumin, though the production data and quality metrics would likely support one. For now, much of Rajasthan's harvest continues to flow through Unjha's APMC — where it may well end up sold under a Gujarat brand.

The spice battle, like the desert wind, shows no signs of settling.
nri_angle: For millions of Indians abroad who rely on jeera as a kitchen staple, the GI tag battle between Gujarat and Rajasthan could reshape pricing and authenticity claims for cumin sold in international markets.
author: Diaspora Desk
